lead: A digital controller reads the error only at fixed instants, T seconds apart, and computes the control from a difference equation. A microprocessor or PLC cannot integrate continuously, so the PID law is rewritten as a sum and a difference. The sampler takes e(kT); the zero-order hold keeps u[k] constant until the next sample. This is the normal form of PID in motor drives, temperature loops, power converters and PLCs. The gains keep their usual meanings, but T now enters every calculation, so a wrong T changes the effective controller.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.2 for P, I and D action, and the rise-time definition from Unit 2 for choosing T.

sections.h3: The sampled loop and the positional form

blocks.text: A sampled-data loop has a continuous plant and a discrete controller. The error is e(t) = r(t) − y(t), where r(t) is the reference and y(t) is the measured output. Every T seconds the sampler closes and the ADC produces e[k] = e(kT), for k = 0, 1, 2, ... T is the sampling period in seconds. The digital PID computes u[k], the control at sample k, and the zero-order hold (ZOH) keeps u(t) = u[k] for kT ≤ t < (k+1)T.

blocks.where: u[k] is the control at sample k; e[k] = e(kT) is the error at that sample; K<sub>p</sub> is dimensionless; K<sub>i</sub> is in s<sup>−1</sup>; K<sub>d</sub> is in s; T is the sampling period in s; and e[−1] = 0.

blocks.text: The first term is present error, the second is accumulated past error, and the third is the recent trend. The sum uses rectangular integration; the difference is a backward derivative. Set e[−1] = 0 at start-up. K<sub>p</sub> is dimensionless, K<sub>i</sub> is in s<sup>−1</sup>, and K<sub>d</sub> is in s, so every term has the same output unit.
The figure shows the order: sum, sampler, PID, ZOH, plant, sensor. The sampler and PID are the new parts; the ZOH is a register and DAC. The sensor and plant remain continuous.

sections.h3: Velocity form, windup and derivative kick

blocks.text: Positional form gives the absolute control u[k]. Velocity form gives the change in control. The old sum disappears; only three errors are stored. Velocity form gives bumpless transfer when switching from manual to automatic, because the output moves from its present value.
Δu[k] = K<sub>p</sub>(e[k] − e[k−1]) + K<sub>i</sub>T e[k] + (K<sub>d</sub>/T)(e[k] − 2e[k−1] + e[k−2])
blocks.where: Δu[k] = u[k] − u[k−1]; set e[−1] = e[−2] = 0 at start-up; other symbols are as in the positional form.

blocks.text: Integral windup is the growth of the sum while the actuator is saturated. The controller keeps adding error that the plant cannot answer, so the output overshoots when the error reverses. Anti-windup clamps the sum, stops integration, or back-calculates from the actual actuator output. Derivative kick is a large derivative term caused by a step in the reference. Use derivative on the measurement y[k], or filter the derivative.
The positional form is easier to read; the velocity form is safer in code with saturation. Both use the same K<sub>p</sub>, K<sub>i</sub>, K<sub>d</sub> and T.

Two standard substitutions replace s with an expression in z<sup>−1</sup>, where z<sup>−1</sup> means a delay of one sample. Backward difference uses s ≈ (1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)/T. Tustin uses s ≈ (2/T)(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)/(1 + z<sup>−1</sup>). Backward difference is simple. Tustin maps the frequency axis more accurately and is preferred when phase error matters.

Choose T small compared with the closed-loop rise time, often T ≤ rise time/10 to rise time/20. Small T improves resolution but costs computation and amplifies sensor noise in the derivative term. An anti-alias filter before the ADC is standard. The same rule applies when a PLC scans a slow temperature loop or a drive controls a motor.
If T is too large, the discrete loop behaves like a low-resolution system: extra phase lag, limit cycles, and poor disturbance rejection.

figure.caption: The sampler takes e[k] every 0.1 s, the digital PID uses Kp=2, Ki=3 s−1 and Kd=0.5 s, and the ZOH holds u[k] for 0.1 s. Notice that the feedback path stays continuous until the sensor output is sampled again.

spec.aria: A reference and feedback meet at a sum, the error is sampled every 0.1 s, a digital PID computes u[k], a zero-order hold feeds the plant, and the sensor closes the loop.

examples.question: A digital PID has K<sub>p</sub>=2, K<sub>i</sub>=3 s<sup>−1</sup>, K<sub>d</sub>=0.5 s and T=0.1 s. The errors are e[0]=1, e[1]=0.5, e[2]=0.2. Find u[2] using the positional form.
steps: Write the data with units: K<sub>p</sub>=2, K<sub>i</sub>=3 s<sup>−1</sup>, K<sub>d</sub>=0.5 s, T=0.1 s, e[0]=1, e[1]=0.5, e[2]=0.2.
examples.answer: u[2] = −0.59 in the controller output unit, for example volts.
examples.check:
kp = 2.0
ki = 3.0
kd = 0.5
T = 0.1
e = [1.0, 0.5, 0.2]
p = kp * e[2]
i = ki * T * sum(e)
d = (kd / T) * (e[2] - e[1])
u = p + i + d
print(round(p, 2))
print(round(i, 2))
print(round(d, 2))
print(round(u, 2))

traps: Forgetting T in the integral term: use K<sub>i</sub>TΣe[j], not K<sub>i</sub>Σe[j]. With T=0.1 s the error is a factor of 10.

Forgetting to divide by T in the derivative term: use (K<sub>d</sub>/T)(e[k]−e[k−1]), not K<sub>d</sub>(e[k]−e[k−1]). With T = 0.1 s the derivative term comes out ten times too small, so the damping is lost.
Using continuous gains after changing T: the effective integral gain is K<sub>i</sub>T and the effective derivative gain is K<sub>d</sub>/T, so retune when T changes.
Ignoring derivative kick and integral windup: a reference step can saturate the actuator, and the sum can keep growing while saturated.
Confusing positional and velocity forms: positional gives u[k]; velocity gives Δu[k]=u[k]−u[k−1]. The examiner may ask which one needs the old sum.

quiz.q: Define T, e[k] and u[k] in a digital PID.
quiz.a: T is the sampling period in s; e[k]=e(kT) is the error at sample k; u[k] is the control held over the next T seconds.

quiz.q: Why is a zero-order hold needed between the digital PID and a continuous plant?
quiz.a: The PID output exists only at sample instants. The ZOH holds each value constant for T seconds so the plant receives a continuous command.

quiz.q: A digital PID has Kp=1.5, Ki=2 s−1, Kd=0.2 s, T=0.2 s. Errors are e[0]=0.8, e[1]=0.4, e[2]=0.1. Find u[2].
T is increased from 0.1 s to 1 s while Kp, Ki, Kd stay fixed. What happens to the integral and derivative actions per sample?
quiz.a: Integral step size KiT grows ten times, so integral action becomes coarse and windup is faster. Derivative gain Kd/T falls ten times, so damping weakens; the loop can oscillate.

quiz.q: Give one advantage of velocity form over positional form.
quiz.a: It outputs only the change, so manual-to-auto transfer is bumpless and the integral sum need not be stored; anti-windup is simpler.

quiz.q: Using the data of the worked example, find Δu[2] by the velocity form.
Name the two common discretization methods for PID.
A step change in reference causes a large derivative spike. Give one fix.
quiz.a: Take derivative on the measured output y[k] instead of error, or filter the derivative term; this removes derivative kick.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial PID blocks add anti-windup, derivative filtering, bumpless transfer and gain scheduling; PLC and drive manuals document these. Digital control theory moves to z-transform models and pole placement; see Unit 6, State Space Analysis, for that route. Search terms: velocity PID, Tustin discretization, integral windup, bumpless transfer.
